summary: Recommends that Internet-facing servers log the source port number and accurate timestamps, not just the client IP address. Address sharing after IPv4 exhaustion means many users can share one address, so the port and time are needed to identify who did what. This is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: When many customers share one public Internet address, that address no longer shows who sent a request. This memo asks servers that already record the incoming address to also record the source port and an accurate timestamp, so a connection can be traced back to one person.

questions: what is carrier grade nat logging
what should internet facing servers log
subtitle: Internet-facing servers should log source port and an accurate timestamp, not just the client IP address.

tldr.problem: After IPv4 exhaustion, several customers can share one public IPv4 address, so the address alone no longer shows who made a connection.
tldr.mechanism: Internet-facing servers that log incoming IP addresses should also log the source port, a timestamp accurate to the second from a traceable time source, and the transport protocol and destination port when the application uses several.
tldr.outcome: An operator that shares addresses can then match a logged connection to one subscriber when handling abuse or public safety requests.

facts.label: Timestamp accuracy
facts.value: To the second or better, in UTC

today: RFC 6302 is Best Current Practice 162 and has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why the Address Alone Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The global IPv4 address free pool at IANA was exhausted in February 2011. Service providers will often have little choice but to share IPv4 global addresses among multiple customers, using address translation or sharing such as NAT44, NAT64 or DS-Lite.

In the past, knowing the external global IP address was enough to identify a subscriber of interest. With address sharing, the external public address of a session alone is no longer sufficient to identify customers unambiguously. This document is about logging on Internet-facing servers, not about logging on carrier-grade NAT or other address sharing tools.
sections.plainLanguage: With address sharing, one public address stands for many customers. A server that records only the address cannot say which customer was involved.

sections.title: What Servers Should Log
sections.content:
It is RECOMMENDED as best current practice that Internet-facing servers that log incoming IP addresses also log:

  • The source port number.
  • A timestamp, RECOMMENDED in UTC, accurate to the second, from a traceable time source such as NTP.
  • The transport protocol (usually TCP or UDP) and destination port number, when the server application is defined to use multiple transports or multiple ports.

Examples of such servers include web servers and email servers. The advice also applies to devices such as load-balancers that log incoming connections on behalf of actual servers, and to both IPv4 and IPv6, if only for consistency and code simplification.
sections.plainLanguage: Along with the sender's address, a server should record which source port was used and exactly when the connection arrived. If the service uses more than one transport or port, it should record those too.

sections.title: Timestamps and Port Reuse
sections.content:
Carrier-grade NATs may have different policies to recycle ports: some may reuse a port almost immediately, others may wait several minutes. Servers cannot know how fast ports will be reused, so they should log timestamps using a reasonably accurate clock, with the recommended accuracy to the second or better.

UTC is preferred to local time with a UTC offset or time zone, because that extra information can be lost in the reporting chain. The recommendations do not require any change in the way logging is performed, such as which packets are examined and logged. Data-retention policies are out of scope, although protecting logs matters: if logs are tampered with, evidence could be destroyed.
sections.plainLanguage: A port number can be given to a different customer a moment later, so the exact time is what separates two connections. UTC is preferred because an offset can be lost when records are passed along.

sections.title: ISPs and Security Considerations
sections.content:
ISPs deploying IP address sharing techniques should also deploy a corresponding logging architecture to keep records of the relation between a customer's identity and the IP and port resources used, but recommendations on that topic are out of scope for this document.

The security consideration is that without the source port number and accurate timestamp, operators deploying any address sharing technique will not be able to identify customers unambiguously when dealing with abuse or public safety queries.
sections.plainLanguage: The point is public safety and abuse handling: without the port and the time, an operator cannot tell which customer to ask about. The memo does not cover how ISPs should keep those records themselves.
